subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Osmosis is the net movement of water:
choices: Across a partially permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration
Across any membrane, from a higher to a lower solute concentration, by diffusion
Through channel proteins against its own concentration gradient using ATP
Of solute particles from high to low concentration in a solution
items.note: Water moves passively towards the higher solute concentration (lower water potential), through the membrane and aquaporins.

items.stem: An animal cell placed in a strongly hypotonic solution will:
choices: Lose water and shrink
Stay unchanged in volume
Gain solutes by active transport
Take in water and may burst
items.note: Hypotonic = lower solute concentration outside, so water enters. Without a wall, animal cells can lyse.

items.stem: Why are solutions given into the blood in hospitals made isotonic?
choices: To kill any bacteria present in the patient's blood
To stop blood cells gaining or losing water by osmosis
To raise blood pressure quickly
To provide energy for respiration
items.note: Isotonic saline has the same solute concentration as body fluids, so cells neither swell nor shrink.

items.stem: Water is a good solvent for ions and polar molecules because:
choices: It has a high specific heat capacity
It is less dense as a solid than as a liquid
Its polar molecules form shells around them
It has strong covalent bonds
items.note: Solvation: partial charges of water attract ions and polar groups, surrounding and separating them.

items.stem: A plant cell placed in a concentrated sugar solution becomes plasmolysed. This means:
choices: The cell wall bursts as water floods into the vacuole
The membrane pulls away from the wall as the vacuole loses water
The cell becomes fully turgid
The cell takes up sugar until it is isotonic
items.note: Water leaves by osmosis; the protoplast shrinks away from the wall. The wall itself stays intact.

items.stem: Potato cylinders are placed in sucrose solutions for 24 hours. Mass does not change at 0.30 mol dm⁻³. This indicates that:
choices: The potato cells are dead at this concentration
Sucrose has entered the potato cells by active transport
The potato tissue is isotonic with 0.30 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
Water potential inside is higher than outside
items.note: No net osmosis means equal water potential/solute concentration. Plot % change in mass and read the x-intercept.

items.stem: What is the water potential of pure water at atmospheric pressure?
choices: −100 kPa
100 kPa
It depends on temperature only
0 kPa
items.note: By definition, pure water at standard pressure has Ψ = 0. Adding solutes makes Ψ negative.

items.stem: A plant cell has solute potential −800 kPa and pressure potential +300 kPa. Its water potential is:
choices: −500 kPa
+500 kPa
−300 kPa

items.stem: The cell above (Ψ = −500 kPa) is placed in a solution with Ψ = −700 kPa. What happens?
choices: Water enters the cell
No net movement
Water leaves the cell
Solute enters the cell
items.note: Water moves from higher (−500) to lower (−700) water potential, so out of the cell.

items.stem: A fully turgid plant cell in pure water has a water potential of 0 kPa because:
choices: Its solute potential has become zero
Water has stopped moving across its membrane completely
All solutes have diffused out of its vacuole into the pure water around it
Its pressure potential has risen to equal its solute potential in size
items.note: At full turgor Ψp = −Ψs, so Ψ = 0, equal to pure water. Water still crosses the membrane, but with no net flow.

items.stem: Animal cells lack a cell wall. Which statement about their water potential is correct?
choices: Pressure potential is close to zero, so water potential ≈ solute potential
Pressure potential is always very high
Water potential is always positive, because water enters freely by osmosis
Solute potential is always zero
items.note: With no wall to push back, little pressure builds, so Ψ ≈ Ψs. This is why animal cells burst rather than become turgid.

items.stem: Compare the effects of a hypotonic solution on an animal cell and a plant cell.
markscheme: Both take in water by osmosis (1)
Animal cell swells and may burst (lysis) (1)
Plant cell becomes turgid but does not burst (1)
Cell wall resists expansion / pressure potential builds (1)
items.tactic: Comparison: one shared point, then paired differences with the reason.

items.stem: Explain how pressure potential and solute potential together determine the direction of water movement into a plant cell.
markscheme: Water potential = solute potential + pressure potential (1)
Solutes lower water potential, drawing water in (1)
As water enters, the wall exerts pressure, raising pressure potential (1)
Water moves until water potential is equal inside and outside (1)
items.tactic: Use Ψ = Ψs + Ψp and describe how each term changes over time.

items.stem: Cell X has Ψs = −1200 kPa and Ψp = +500 kPa. Adjacent cell Y has Ψs = −900 kPa and Ψp = +400 kPa. Determine the direction of water movement between them, showing your working.
markscheme: Water moves from Y to X (1)
because water moves from higher to lower water potential (1)
items.tactic: Show both sums before deciding; quote the rule.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Cylinders of an invented root vegetable were placed in sucrose solutions for 24 h. % change in mass: 0.0 mol dm⁻³ +18%; 0.2 +7%; 0.4 −3%; 0.6 −11%; 0.8 −17%.
(a) Estimate the sucrose concentration that is isotonic with the tissue. (b) Explain the result at 0.8 mol dm⁻³. (c) Explain why % change in mass, not change in mass, is used. (d) Suggest why the change between 0.6 and 0.8 is smaller than between 0 and 0.2.
markscheme: (a) Between 0.2 and 0.4: about 0.34 mol dm⁻³ (interpolation; accept 0.32–0.36) (1)
(b) Solution has lower water potential than the cells, so water leaves by osmosis and mass falls (1)
(c) Cylinders have different starting masses, so % allows fair comparison (1)
(d) Cells become plasmolysed / little water left in vacuoles to lose / cell walls limit shrinkage (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
